ASNT Level III consulting: what an outsourced Level III does under SNT-TC-1A

An outsourced ASNT Level III does six things for an employer under SNT-TC-1A. They write and maintain the written practice. They prepare and approve procedures. They approve techniques for specific jobs. They prepare, administer or oversee qualification examinations. They review certification records. They support internal and client audits. The employer stays the certifying authority and owns the records. The Level III supplies the technical judgement and the signatures behind them.

This section goes through each duty in turn: what gets produced, what an auditor looks for and where programs usually fail. If you are comparing providers across the country, the US consulting hub covers that. To scope your own program, talk to a Level III.

Duty 1: the written practice

The written practice is the employer's own controlled document. SNT-TC-1A supplies recommended values. Once the employer adopts them, "should" becomes "shall", and the employer is audited against what its document says. The 2024 edition of SNT-TC-1A is the current one, and it replaced the 2020 edition. A written practice that still cites an older edition should be reviewed, even if nothing else has changed.

A complete written practice covers, method by method and level by level:

  • The methods and techniques in the program, for example UT split into thickness, shear wave, PAUT and TOFD where the training and examinations differ.
  • Training content and hours for each level, and what counts as acceptable training evidence.
  • Experience requirements, and how experience hours are logged and signed.
  • Examination types, who prepares and administers them, how they are graded and when a failed candidate may retake.
  • Vision examination requirements and how often they are repeated.
  • Certification records: what each file holds, who signs and how certificates are controlled.
  • Recertification intervals and the evidence accepted for recertification.
  • Use of an outside agency or outside Level III, if any, and the limits of that arrangement.
  • Suspension, revocation and reinstatement of certification.

The outsourced Level III drafts this, walks the employer's managers through it and keeps it current. In practice, the written practice changes when you add a method, when a client spec adds a requirement, when a new edition is adopted, or when an audit finds a gap. Each change gets a revision number, a date and a record of what changed. If your document has had the same revision for years while the company has added PAUT and a new client base, it is out of date even if nobody has complained yet.

For a clause-by-clause guide to the document itself, see NDT written practice development.

Duty 2: procedures and technique approval

A procedure says how a method is applied to a class of work under a named code. A technique sheet applies that procedure to a specific part: this nozzle, this thickness, this weld configuration, this probe and wedge. The Level III prepares or reviews and approves both. The difference matters, because most field problems come from the gap between them.

A procedure the Level III will sign usually states:

  • Scope, materials and thickness range.
  • The governing code and its edition, for example ASME Section V with the referencing construction code, AWS D1.1 or API 1104.
  • Personnel qualification, by reference to the written practice.
  • Equipment, probes or sources, and calibration requirements.
  • Reference blocks or standards, and how system performance is checked.
  • Scanning or examination technique, coverage and surface condition.
  • Evaluation and acceptance criteria, cited to the clause that sets them.
  • Reporting content and record retention.

Technique approval is where an outsourced Level III earns the fee. A technician arrives at a branch connection, a thick-to-thin transition or a weld with limited access, and the general procedure does not quite fit. The right answer is a technique sheet, approved before the reportable work, showing the scan plan, coverage and any limitations. The wrong answer is an improvised setup that gets written up as "per procedure". The engagement should define how field requests reach the Level III and how fast they get an answer. A technique request that waits a week gets bypassed.

Where a referencing code or client requires a procedure to be demonstrated, the Level III plans the demonstration, witnesses it or has it witnessed, and files the result with the procedure. For gas pipeline welds, 49 CFR 192.243 requires nondestructive testing to follow written procedures and be done by persons trained and qualified in those procedures and the equipment used, so pipeline clients usually ask for both documents side by side.

Duty 3: examinations

Under SNT-TC-1A, Level I and Level II candidates take a general, a specific and a practical examination for each method. The recommended pass mark is at least 70 percent on each examination and at least 80 percent composite. The Level III prepares or approves the examinations, administers them or oversees whoever does, and keeps them secure.

  • General examination. Method principles, capabilities and limitations, equipment and discontinuities. Drawn from a controlled question bank, not from a set of questions that has circulated for years.
  • Specific examination. The employer's own procedures, equipment, codes and product forms. A specific examination that never mentions your procedures is not specific.
  • Practical examination. Hands-on setup, calibration, examination, recording and evaluation, on specimens that represent the work. A pipe-weld crew should be examined on pipe welds, not a flat plate.

Level III candidates are examined differently, with basic, method and specific examinations. Many employers accept an ASNT NDT Level III certificate as the evidence for the basic and method parts and set their own specific examination. The written practice should say which.

When the Level III is remote, examinations still have to be controlled. That means papers released for a set sitting, a named proctor, practical examinations scheduled for a site visit or witnessed by a qualified person, and grade sheets signed and returned to the employer's file. Some employers also use Practical NDT, a 3D skills simulator, so candidates can practise setups before the practical. Practice does not replace the practical examination.

Duty 4: record review and audits

A certification file is the evidence that the written practice was followed for one person. Auditors sample these files first, because a weak file means a weak program. The outsourced Level III reviews them on a cycle, not just before an audit.

Record elementWhat the Level III checksCommon finding
Training hoursHours per method and level match the written practice, with the source and datesA course certificate with no hours, or hours for the wrong level
Experience hoursA signed log by method, adding up to the written practice minimum before certificationExperience claimed in total, not by method
ExaminationsEach grade recorded, composite calculated, examiner named, date before certificationComposite score only, with the separate grades missing
VisionNear-vision and color checks current at the interval the written practice setsAn expired vision record on an otherwise valid certificate
CertificationMethod, level, technique limits, date and the certifying authority's signatureA certificate signed by someone who has left the company
RecertificationDue dates tracked, evidence on file before expiryCertificates that expired quietly while the technician kept working

Audits come in three kinds. Internal audits are run by the Level III against the written practice and procedures, usually once a year and after any major change. Client and prequalification audits are run by operators and EPCs against their own checklist. Registrar audits look at the quality system around the NDT program. For each, the Level III prepares the evidence, runs a mock audit where useful and answers technical questions on the day. Corrective actions are tracked to closure, and the written practice is revised if the finding was systemic.

Expiry dates, vision dates and recertification triggers are easier to keep when a system warns you before they lapse. See NDT personnel certification tracking in Atlantis ERP. For the findings we see most often in written practice audits, read common written practice audit findings.

Who does what in an outsourced Level III arrangement

Most disputes in these arrangements come from a task nobody thought was theirs. Write the split into the written practice and the engagement letter. This is the split we use as a starting point.

The engagement letter should also state the methods covered, the review cycle, response time for technique requests, site days, who holds the question banks and what happens on termination. On termination, every document the Level III prepared stays with the employer. That one line prevents the worst handovers.

Taking over a program from a previous Level III

Many of our engagements start because a Level III left. The certificates already issued do not become void the day they leave. But the program needs a new technical authority before the next approval, examination or audit. This is the order we work in.

  1. Inventory. Collect the written practice, every procedure and technique sheet, the question banks and every certification file. Find out what is in someone's personal email or laptop.
  2. Check the written practice names the right person. Revise it to name the new Level III arrangement and the date it took effect.
  3. Review open approvals. Procedures and techniques in use are reviewed and re-approved under the new Level III where needed. Anything that cannot be traced to an approval is pulled until it is reviewed.
  4. Review the certification files. Sort them into valid, valid but with gaps to fix, and not supportable. Gaps are usually missing grades or lapsed vision records.
  5. Plan recertifications. List every certificate falling due in the next year and schedule examinations or recertification evidence ahead of the dates.
  6. Tell your clients. Major clients expect to hear when your Level III changes. Send the revised written practice before they ask.

Done in this order, a handover rarely interrupts field work. Left alone, it usually surfaces at the worst moment, during a client audit or a turnaround mobilisation. For state-specific client expectations, see the hubs for Texas, Louisiana and Pennsylvania.

Finding a certified NDT person for steel mill rolls

Steel mills inspect work rolls and backup rolls in the roll shop, usually after grinding and before a roll goes back into a stand. Two methods do most of the work. Eddy current (ET) finds surface cracks and surface damage. Ultrasonic testing (UT) finds subsurface defects and, on composite rolls, checks the bond between shell and core. Many roll grinders carry automated ET and UT systems, but someone still has to set them up, verify them against reference standards and decide what an indication means.

The person you are looking for is an SNT-TC-1A Level II in UT, ET or both, certified by their employer, working to a roll-specific procedure approved by a Level III. That gives you two routes.

  • Certify your own roll shop people. Most mills have experienced roll shop operators already running the equipment. A Level III writes UT and ET sections into the mill's written practice, prepares a roll procedure with reference standards and acceptance limits agreed with the mill's engineers, and examines the operators. They then work as certified personnel, not just machine operators.
  • Use an inspection contractor. For periodic checks, disputed rolls or a backlog, a contractor sends certified UT and ET technicians who work to an approved procedure. Ask to see that procedure and the technicians' certification records before work starts.

Either way, the procedure is the part most mills lack. Acceptance limits for roll defects are often set by the mill or the roll maker rather than by a public code, so they have to be written down and approved. Steel and heavy fabrication are concentrated in states such as Indiana and Ohio, where our state pages cover local delivery. Atlantis provides both routes: Level III procedure and certification work, and UT and ET inspection by ASNT-certified technicians under Level III oversight. Request an inspection quote for roll inspection, or talk to a Level III about certifying your roll shop.

Frequently asked questions

What does ASNT Level III consulting cover day to day?

On a retainer, most of the work is small and steady: approving technique sheets for field requests, revising procedures when a client spec changes, reviewing new hires' files, preparing examinations and recertifications as they fall due, and answering technical questions. Larger pieces, such as a written practice rewrite or an audit, are scheduled as projects within the retainer.

Who owns the certification when an outside Level III runs the examinations?

The employer. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer is the certifying authority and keeps the records. The outside Level III prepares, administers or oversees and grades the examinations, and recommends or signs where the written practice says so.

Can an NDT Level 3 consultant run examinations remotely?

General and specific examinations can be run remotely with controlled release and a named proctor. Practical examinations need a qualified person present with the specimens, either the Level III on a site visit or a designated examiner the written practice allows.

How often should the written practice be reviewed?

At least once a year, and whenever you add a method, adopt a new SNT-TC-1A or code edition, take on a client with new requirements or close an audit finding that points to the document. Each revision should be numbered, dated and summarised.

What should be in every technician's certification file?

Training hours with source and dates, a signed experience log by method, each examination grade and the composite, current vision records, the certificate with method, level and any technique limits, the certifying authority's signature and the recertification due date.

Where can I find a certified NDT person to work on rolls in steel mills?

Look for an SNT-TC-1A Level II in UT and ET working to a roll-specific procedure approved by a Level III. You can certify your own roll shop operators under your written practice, or bring in an inspection contractor whose technicians are certified and who will show you the procedure first.

What happens to existing certificates when we change Level III?

They do not lapse automatically. The new Level III reviews the files, confirms which are fully supported and which need gaps fixed, re-approves procedures in use and plans the recertifications that fall due. The written practice is revised to name the new arrangement.

Does holding an ASNT NDT Level III certificate make someone our Level III?

Not by itself. The employer certifies its Level III under its own written practice. Many employers accept the ASNT NDT Level III certificate as evidence for the basic and method examinations and add their own specific examination.

Ready to hand over the Level III work? Talk to a Level III. Send the current written practice and the methods you use, and we will come back with a scope. For training to the hours your written practice sets, see NDT training in the USA, or go back to the consulting overview.
